source.title: Say What You Mean, Kindly
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on the Better Health Channel (Victoria), the Centre for Clinical Interventions (Western Australia) and Mayo Clinic guidance on assertive communication.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: Better Health Channel (Victoria State Government), Assertiveness, https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/assertiveness; Centre for Clinical Interventions, Assertiveness self-help resources, https://www.cci.health.wa.gov.au/Resources/Looking-After-Yourself/Assertiveness; Mayo Clinic, Being assertive: Reduce stress, communicate better, https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/stress-management/in-depth/assertive/art-20044644

cards.title: Saying what you mean, kindly, is a skill you can learn
cards.body:
Many of us were taught that being nice means going along with things. So we drop hints, say 'it's fine' when it isn't, or bottle things up until they burst out. None of that helps anyone, including the people we're trying to protect.

This guide is about a middle path: saying clearly what you think, need and feel, while staying respectful. It covers the four common styles of speaking, asking directly, saying no, setting boundaries, cutting hedges and needless apologies, disagreeing well and naming feelings.

Think of a flatmate who never washes up. You can stew, snap, leave passive notes, or calmly ask. Only the last one has a real chance of working.
cards.apply_it: Notice one moment today when you said 'it's fine' or 'whatever you think' but didn't mean it. Just notice it for now.

quiz.question: What does this guide mean by saying what you mean kindly?
options: Always agreeing to keep the peace
Being clear about your needs while respecting others
Winning every argument
Dropping hints until people guess
quiz.explanation: The aim is a middle path: honest and direct about what you think and need, while staying respectful of the other person.

cards.title: There are four common ways people speak up, or don't
cards.body:
People often fall into one of four styles. Passive: putting others first and staying quiet about your own needs. Aggressive: pushing your needs at the expense of others, through blame, volume or pressure. Passive-aggressive: feeling angry but showing it sideways, through sulking, sarcasm or 'forgetting'. Assertive: stating your needs and views honestly while respecting the other person's.

Imagine a colleague keeps taking credit for your work. Passive is saying nothing. Aggressive is calling them out in front of everyone. Passive-aggressive is a cold, clipped reply all week. Assertive is a private word: 'I'd like my part of the project credited to me.'

Most of us use all four at times, depending on who we're with and how tired we are.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent small conflict. Which of the four styles did you use? Name it honestly, without judging yourself.

quiz.question: A friend is annoyed but says nothing, then replies to messages with one-word answers for days. Which style is this?
options: Assertive
Passive
Aggressive
Passive-aggressive
quiz.explanation: Anger shown indirectly, through coldness or sulking rather than words, is the passive-aggressive style.

cards.title: Staying quiet to keep the peace usually costs you later
cards.body:
The passive style can feel kind and safe. You avoid fuss, you don't upset anyone, and you seem easy-going. But your needs don't disappear just because you don't say them.

Say you always end up hosting family for Sunday lunch and you're worn out. If you never mention it, nothing changes. Over time, tiredness turns into resentment, and resentment leaks out in other ways. Others may also feel confused when you finally snap over something small.

Being passive also takes away other people's chance to help. Your sister might happily take a turn hosting, but she can't offer what she doesn't know you need. Speaking up is often more generous than staying silent.
cards.apply_it: Pick one small thing you've been quietly putting up with. Write down, in one sentence, what you would like to be different.

quiz.question: Why can staying quiet about your needs backfire?
options: Resentment builds and others can't help with what they don't know
It always makes people respect you more
It means you never feel tired
It forces others to guess correctly
quiz.explanation: Unspoken needs tend to build into resentment, and people can't respond to problems they haven't been told about.

cards.title: Being aggressive may win the point but it damages the relationship
cards.body:
Aggression is not only shouting. It includes interrupting, sarcasm, blaming, 'you always' statements and pushing until the other person gives in. It can get quick results, which is why it's tempting.

Picture a parent telling a teenager, 'You're so lazy, you never help!' The teen might clear the table, but they'll feel attacked, defend themselves or shut down. Next time, they'll be braced for a fight before you even speak.

At work, a manager who barks orders may get tasks done but lose trust and honest feedback. People stop telling them about problems. The aim of speaking up is not to beat someone. It's to be heard and to keep a relationship you can still work with tomorrow.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel the urge to say 'you always' or 'you never', pause and describe one specific event instead.

quiz.question: Which of these is an aggressive way to raise a problem?
options: 'Could we talk about the bins tonight?'
'I'd like us to share the cooking more.'
'You never lift a finger, you're useless.'
quiz.explanation: Labels like 'useless' and sweeping words like 'never' attack the person, which tends to make them defensive rather than cooperative.

cards.title: Passive-aggressive messages leave everyone guessing and annoyed
cards.body:
Passive-aggressive behaviour is anger that comes out sideways. It sounds like 'Fine, do what you want', 'Per my last email', a heavy sigh while loading the dishwasher, or a sticky note saying 'Some of us like clean mugs!'

It can feel safer than direct conflict because you can always deny it: 'I didn't mean anything by it.' But the other person still picks up the hostility, without any clear request to act on. So the problem stays, and now there's tension too.

If you notice yourself sighing loudly, going quiet or being 'jokingly' sharp, it's usually a sign there's something you haven't said. Ask yourself: what do I actually want here? Then say that instead.
cards.apply_it: If you catch yourself sighing, sulking or making a pointed joke today, ask: what do I really want? Then say it in one plain sentence.

quiz.question: What's the main problem with a note saying 'Some of us like clean mugs!'?
options: It's too polite
It's too long to read
It uses too many facts
It shows annoyance but makes no clear, direct request
quiz.explanation: Passive-aggressive messages signal irritation without saying what you want, so the problem stays and resentment grows.

cards.title: Assertiveness means respecting yourself and the other person at once
cards.body:
Being assertive is not being bossy or loud. It means saying honestly what you think, feel or want, in a calm way that also respects the other person's right to their own view.

In practice it sounds like: 'I'd like to finish this before taking on the new task', or 'I see it differently, can I explain why?' Your voice is steady, your words are clear, and you're not attacking or apologising for existing.

Assertiveness doesn't guarantee you get what you want. Your partner may still prefer the beach to the mountains. But you've said your piece, they know where you stand, and you can work it out together. That clarity tends to build trust over time.
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence you need to say to someone this week, starting with 'I'd like' or 'I think'. Keep it calm and specific.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes assertiveness?
options: Saying your needs clearly while respecting the other person
Getting your way every time
Never disagreeing with anyone
Speaking louder than others
quiz.explanation: Assertiveness balances honesty about your own needs with respect for others. It doesn't promise you'll always get your way.

cards.title: Hints rarely work because people are busy with their own thoughts
cards.body:
Hinting feels gentler than asking. 'It's getting a bit messy in here', 'I suppose someone should book the restaurant', 'Wow, you're really busy lately.' We hope the other person will decode it and act.

But most people are wrapped up in their own day. They hear the words, not the hidden request. Your partner may simply agree the room is messy and carry on. Then you feel ignored, and they have no idea why you're cross.

Hints also make it easy for the other person to miss, and for you to feel hurt. A clear ask, such as 'Could you tidy the living room before dinner?', is actually kinder, because it gives them a fair chance to say yes.
cards.apply_it: Catch one hint you're about to drop today and turn it into a direct question starting with 'Could you...?'

quiz.question: Why is a direct request often kinder than a hint?
options: It makes them guess harder
It sounds more dramatic
It gives the other person a fair, clear chance to help
It avoids any chance of a no
quiz.explanation: A direct request removes the guessing, so the other person knows exactly what you'd like and can actually respond.

cards.title: Ask for exactly what you want, not a vague version of it
cards.body:
Vague requests get vague results. 'Can you help more around the house?' or 'I need more support at work' sound clear to you, but the other person has to guess what 'more' means.

Be specific about what, when and how much. 'Could you do the school run on Tuesdays and Thursdays?' is much easier to agree to. At work, 'Could we have a 15-minute check-in each Monday?' beats 'I'd like more feedback.'

It helps to work out your request before you speak. Ask yourself: if they said yes, what exactly would they do differently? If you can picture it, you can say it. Specific requests also make it easier to notice and thank people when they follow through.
cards.apply_it: Turn one vague wish ('more help', 'more time') into a request with a what and a when. Say it to the person today.

quiz.question: Which request is most likely to get a useful response?
options: 'Can you be more helpful?'
'Could you put the bins out on Sunday nights?'
'I need you to try harder.'
'You know what I need.'
quiz.explanation: A specific request says what and when, so the other person knows exactly what a yes would involve.

cards.title: Turn a complaint into a request about the future
cards.body:
Complaints look backwards: 'You were late again', 'Nobody told me about the meeting.' They're often fair, but they leave the other person feeling blamed and unsure what to do next.

A request looks forwards. 'Could you text me if you're running more than ten minutes late?' or 'Please add me to the invite list for project meetings.' The same frustration is there, but now there's a clear way to fix it.

You can still mention what happened briefly, then move to the ask: 'I missed the meeting because I wasn't on the invite. Could you add me?' This keeps the focus on solving the problem rather than on who was at fault, which most people respond to far better.
cards.apply_it: Think of a complaint you've made more than once. Rewrite it as a future request starting with 'Could you...' or 'From now on, please...'

quiz.question: What makes a request more useful than a complaint?
options: It points to a clear action for the future
It lists every past mistake
It proves the other person was wrong
It avoids mentioning the problem at all
quiz.explanation: Requests look forward and give a clear action, which is easier to act on than blame about the past.

cards.title: A simple shape helps: what happened, how it affects you, what you'd like
cards.body:
When you need to raise something tricky, a three-part shape keeps you clear and fair. First, describe what happened, as neutrally as you can. Second, say how it affects you. Third, say what you'd like.

For example: 'When the music is loud after 11, I can't sleep before work. Could you turn it down after 10:30 on weeknights?' Or with a friend: 'When plans change last minute, I feel let down because I've arranged childcare. Could you give me a day's notice?'

The shape stops you rambling, blaming or burying the request. You don't have to use it word for word. It's a scaffold to lean on until speaking up this way feels natural.
cards.apply_it: Draft one tricky conversation using the three parts: what happened, how it affects you, what you'd like. Keep each part to one sentence.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of the simple request shape?
options: What happened, how it affects you, what you'd like
Apology, excuse, compliment
Your opinion, their faults, a warning
quiz.explanation: Describing the situation, its effect on you and your request keeps the message clear, fair and focused on a solution.

cards.title: You're allowed to say no without being a bad person
cards.body:
Many people say yes out of guilt, fear of disappointing others or worry about seeming unhelpful. The result is a full diary, little rest and quiet resentment.

Saying no to a request is not saying no to the person. You can care about your friend and still decline helping them move house this weekend. You can value your job and still say you can't take on another project right now.

Every yes uses up time and energy you could spend elsewhere, including on the people and tasks that matter most. A thoughtful no protects your ability to say a real, willing yes to the things you choose. People generally respect a clear no more than a reluctant yes followed by a cancellation.
cards.apply_it: Look at your week ahead. Find one commitment you agreed to out of guilt and consider whether you can still kindly decline it.

quiz.question: What does saying no to a request mean?
options: You don't care about the person
You'll lose the friendship
You're declining the request, not rejecting the person
You must never ask them for anything again
quiz.explanation: Declining a request is about your time and capacity, not a judgement on the person asking.

cards.title: Say no briefly, without a long list of excuses
cards.body:
When we feel guilty, we tend to over-explain: 'I'd love to, but my mum might visit, and I've got this cold coming on, and work has been mad...' Long excuses invite the other person to solve each one: 'Oh, bring your mum!'

A short, warm no is clearer and kinder. 'Thanks for asking, but I can't make it this time.' Or at work: 'I don't have room for that this week.' You can give one honest reason if you want, but you don't owe a full case.

Keep your tone friendly and your words simple, then stop talking. The pause might feel awkward, but it lets your answer stand. Most people accept a calm no far more easily than we expect.
cards.apply_it: Next time you say no, use one sentence, such as 'Thanks, but I can't this time', and resist adding more reasons.

quiz.question: Why can over-explaining a no backfire?
options: It gives the other person reasons to argue or problem-solve
It makes the no too short
It always sounds rude
It means you have to say yes
quiz.explanation: Each excuse becomes something the other person can try to fix, which turns a simple no into a negotiation.

cards.title: Offer an alternative only when you genuinely want to
cards.body:
A 'no, but' can be lovely: 'I can't come to the party, but could we get coffee next week?' or 'I can't lead the project, but I could review the plan on Friday.' It shows goodwill and keeps the door open.

The trap is offering an alternative just to soften the blow, when you don't really want to do that either. Then you've swapped one unwanted yes for another, and you're back where you started.

Before offering something else, check with yourself: would I be glad to do this? If yes, offer it warmly. If not, a plain, kind no is enough. It's more honest than a half-hearted offer you later regret or quietly cancel.
cards.apply_it: Before offering a 'no, but' this week, ask yourself: would I truly be glad to do this alternative? Only offer it if the answer is yes.

quiz.question: When is offering an alternative to a request a good idea?
options: Always, to avoid seeming rude
Only when the person is upset
Never, as it confuses people
Only when you'd genuinely be glad to do it
quiz.explanation: An alternative is generous when it's real. Offered out of guilt, it just swaps one unwanted commitment for another.

cards.title: You can buy time instead of answering on the spot
cards.body:
Many unwanted yeses happen because we answer too fast. Someone asks, there's a pause, and 'sure' slips out before we've checked our diary or our energy.

It's fine to say, 'Let me check and get back to you by tomorrow.' This works with a boss asking for weekend cover, a relative inviting you to stay, or a neighbour wanting a favour. It gives you space to decide calmly rather than under pressure.

The key is to actually get back to them, and when you said you would. A pause isn't a way to dodge; it's a way to give a considered answer. If the answer is no, you'll say it more clearly having thought it through.
cards.apply_it: Practise a stock phrase today, such as 'Let me check and come back to you by...', and use it on the next request you're unsure about.

quiz.question: What's the point of saying 'Let me check and get back to you'?
options: To avoid ever answering
To give yourself time to decide calmly, then reply
To make the person wait as punishment
To hint that the answer is yes
quiz.explanation: Buying time helps you make a considered decision instead of a rushed yes, as long as you follow up when you promised.

cards.title: A boundary is about what you will do, not what others must do
cards.body:
People sometimes treat boundaries as rules for others: 'You must stop calling me at work.' But you can't control other people. You can only decide what you'll do.

A clearer boundary sounds like: 'I don't take personal calls during work hours. I'll ring you back after six.' Or: 'If the shouting starts, I'll leave the room and we can talk later.' You're not demanding; you're telling them how you'll respond.

This makes boundaries calmer and easier to keep. You don't need the other person's agreement for them to work. With family, friends or colleagues, it shifts the conversation from a power struggle to simple information about what you will and won't do.
cards.apply_it: Think of something that keeps bothering you. Write a boundary that starts with 'I will' or 'I won't', describing your own action.

quiz.question: Which of these is a boundary framed around your own action?
options: 'You have to stop texting me so late.'
'You're so inconsiderate.'
'I don't reply to messages after 10pm; I'll answer in the morning.'
'Everyone thinks you text too much.'
quiz.explanation: A boundary describes what you will do, which you control, rather than demanding that others change.

cards.title: State a boundary once, clearly and calmly, without a lecture
cards.body:
When we finally set a boundary, it's tempting to pour out every past frustration. But a long speech can sound like an attack, and the actual boundary gets lost.

Keep it short and calm. 'I'm not going to discuss my weight. Let's talk about something else.' Or with a colleague: 'I need you to check with me before changing the shared document.' One or two sentences, said in a normal voice, are enough.

You don't need to justify it at length or win the other person over. A boundary is not a debate. If they ask why, you can give a short reason, but you're allowed to simply say, 'It matters to me.'
cards.apply_it: Write the boundary you need in no more than two sentences. Read it aloud and remove any part that sounds like a lecture.

quiz.question: What usually makes a boundary more effective?
options: Stating it briefly and calmly
Raising your voice so they know you're serious
Listing every time the person upset you
Waiting until you're furious
quiz.explanation: A short, calm boundary is easier to hear and harder to argue with than a long list of grievances.

cards.title: Boundaries only work if you follow through on them
cards.body:
If you say you'll leave the room when the arguing gets nasty, but then you stay and argue, the boundary becomes just words. People learn what you do, not just what you say.

Following through doesn't have to be dramatic. If you've said you don't check work email at weekends, don't reply on Saturday, even if it would only take a minute. If you've said you'll leave a family visit by eight, put your coat on at eight.

The first few times might feel awkward, and some people may test it. That's normal. Calm, consistent action shows you meant it, and over time most people adjust. Be kind to yourself if you slip, and simply start again.
cards.apply_it: Choose one boundary you've stated before but not kept. Plan exactly what you'll do the next time it's tested.

quiz.question: Why does following through on a boundary matter?
options: It means you never need to speak again
It makes you seem unpredictable
It punishes the other person
People learn from what you do, not just what you say
quiz.explanation: Consistent action shows your boundary is real. Without it, people learn the words don't mean much.

cards.title: Too much hedging hides what you actually think
cards.body:
Hedges are the little softeners we pile on: 'I just think maybe', 'Sorry, this might be stupid, but', 'I'm not sure, but possibly...' A bit of softening is fine. Too much, and your point disappears.

Compare 'I just wondered if maybe we could possibly look at the budget?' with 'Could we look at the budget?' The second is still polite, but much clearer. In a meeting, 'I recommend we delay the launch' carries more weight than 'This is probably wrong, but maybe we could delay?'

If you're genuinely unsure, say so once and clearly: 'I'm not certain, but my best guess is Thursday.' That's honest. What weakens you is hedging by habit, not real doubt.
cards.apply_it: Before sending your next message, delete the words 'just', 'maybe' and 'sorry' where they aren't needed. Read it again to see if it's clearer.

quiz.question: Which version of a suggestion is clearest while still polite?
options: 'Sorry, this might be silly, but maybe we could...'
'I just wondered if possibly...'
'Could we move the meeting to Thursday?'
'I'm probably wrong, but...'
quiz.explanation: Stripping away habit hedges leaves a clear, polite request that's easy to understand and act on.

cards.title: Save sorry for when you've actually done something wrong
cards.body:
Many people say sorry dozens of times a day: sorry for asking a question, sorry for bumping into a chair, sorry for having an opinion. It becomes a reflex.

The trouble is that constant apologising can make you seem less sure of yourself, and it waters down the word for when you really mean it. 'Sorry to bother you, sorry, just a quick one' tells people you think you're an inconvenience.

Try noticing when you say it. If you haven't done anything wrong, you can usually just drop it: 'Do you have a minute?' instead of 'Sorry, have you got a minute?' Keep your real apologies for real mistakes, and make those sincere and clear.
cards.apply_it: Count how many times you say or type 'sorry' today. For each one, ask: did I actually do anything wrong?

quiz.question: What's the main downside of apologising out of habit?
options: People will think you're rude
It can make you seem unsure and weakens real apologies
It makes conversations shorter
It's against workplace rules
quiz.explanation: Reflex apologies can signal low confidence and dilute the meaning of a genuine apology.

cards.title: Swap a needless sorry for a thank you
cards.body:
A handy trick is to turn many reflex apologies into thanks. Instead of 'Sorry I'm late', try 'Thanks for waiting.' Instead of 'Sorry for going on', try 'Thanks for listening.' Instead of 'Sorry, I made a mistake in that email', try 'Thanks for spotting that.'

This keeps the warmth and acknowledgement, but shifts the focus from your failings to the other person's kindness. It usually leaves both of you feeling better.

It won't fit every situation. If you've genuinely let someone down, a proper apology matters. But for everyday moments, like a friend helping you carry shopping or a colleague answering a question, thank you is often the more accurate and generous phrase.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're about to say a reflex sorry, swap it for a thank you, such as 'Thanks for your patience.'

quiz.question: Which is a good 'thank you' swap for 'Sorry for rambling'?
options: 'Thanks for listening.'
'Sorry, sorry, I'll stop.'
'You should have stopped me.'
'I always ramble, it's awful.'
quiz.explanation: 'Thanks for listening' keeps the warmth while recognising the other person, rather than putting yourself down.

cards.title: Repeating your point calmly can work better than arguing
cards.body:
Sometimes you state your position and the other person keeps pushing: a salesperson, a pushy relative, a colleague wanting you to cover their shift. It's tempting to add more reasons or get annoyed.

The 'broken record' technique means calmly repeating the same short message, perhaps with a brief nod to what they've said. 'I understand it's busy, but I can't cover Saturday.' 'I know you're stuck, but I can't cover Saturday.' Same core line, same calm tone.

You're not being rude; you're being consistent. By not adding new arguments, you give them nothing new to push against. Save this for when someone isn't accepting a clear answer, not for normal back-and-forth discussion.
cards.apply_it: Prepare one short sentence for a request you'll likely face this week. Plan to repeat it calmly if pushed, without adding new excuses.

quiz.question: What is the 'broken record' technique?
options: Shouting until the other person gives up
Ignoring the person completely
Changing your answer each time to keep them guessing
Calmly repeating the same short message when pushed
quiz.explanation: Calmly repeating a short, consistent message avoids getting drawn into argument and makes your answer clear.

cards.title: You can disagree openly and still be respectful
cards.body:
Disagreeing isn't the same as attacking. You can think a friend's holiday plan is too expensive, or a colleague's idea won't work, and say so without damaging the relationship.

Start by showing you've understood: 'So you'd like to fly out on Friday to get the extra day.' Then give your view clearly: 'I see it differently. The Saturday flights are half the price, and I'd rather spend that on the trip.' Stick to the issue and your reasons.

Avoid 'you're wrong' or 'that's ridiculous'. Instead use phrases like 'I see it differently' or 'I have a concern about...' Respectful disagreement often leads to better decisions, because both views get a fair hearing.
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, start with 'I see it differently' and give one clear reason, instead of 'You're wrong.'

quiz.question: Which is a respectful way to disagree?
options: 'That's a ridiculous idea.'
'Whatever, do what you want.'
'I see it differently. Can I explain my concern?'
quiz.explanation: Naming your different view and inviting discussion keeps the focus on the issue, not on attacking the person.

cards.title: Disagree with the idea, not the person
cards.body:
When we disagree, it's easy to slip from the idea to the person: 'That's a silly plan' quickly becomes 'You never think things through.' Once it feels personal, people defend themselves rather than consider your point.

Keep the focus on the specific plan, decision or behaviour. 'I'm worried this timeline doesn't leave room for testing' talks about the work. 'You always rush things' talks about the colleague. At home, 'I don't think the new sofa will fit' is easier to hear than 'You've got no sense of space.'

You can even say something kind about the person while disagreeing with the idea: 'I love that you want to surprise everyone, but I think a big party will stress Mum out.'
cards.apply_it: When you disagree today, check that your sentence is about the plan or action, not the person's character.

quiz.question: Which comment disagrees with the idea rather than the person?
options: 'I think this plan has too many steps for one week.'
'You always overcomplicate things.'
'You clearly didn't think about it.'
'You're hopeless at planning.'
quiz.explanation: Talking about the plan itself invites discussion, while comments about character make people defensive.

cards.title: Name your feelings with real words, not just 'fine'
cards.body:
Many of us use a tiny feelings vocabulary: fine, okay, stressed, annoyed. 'Fine' especially can mean anything from content to furious, which leaves others guessing.

Being more precise helps people understand you. 'I'm disappointed we didn't get time together this weekend' says more than 'Whatever, it's fine.' At work, 'I'm worried about hitting the deadline' is more useful than 'It's all a bit much.'

Try reaching for a more exact word: hurt, left out, overwhelmed, relieved, nervous, embarrassed, grateful. You don't need a big emotional speech. One honest, accurate word often opens up a real conversation, where 'fine' quietly closes it down.
cards.apply_it: When someone asks how you are today, replace 'fine' with one more accurate feeling word, if it feels safe to do so.

quiz.question: Why can saying 'I'm fine' cause problems?
options: It's too emotional
It can hide what you really feel and leave others guessing
It's always a lie
It makes conversations too long
quiz.explanation: 'Fine' covers a huge range of feelings, so a more precise word helps others understand what's really going on.

cards.title: Own your feelings instead of making them someone else's fault
cards.body:
'You made me so angry' puts the other person in charge of your emotions and sounds like an accusation. They'll likely defend themselves rather than listen.

Owning your feeling sounds more like: 'I felt hurt when my birthday wasn't mentioned at dinner.' You're describing your reaction to an event, not passing judgement. It's honest and harder to argue with, because it's your experience.

This doesn't mean the other person has done nothing wrong. It simply opens the door to talking about it calmly. You'll find more on this approach in our conflict guide. Here the key point is simple: say what you felt and what happened, then leave space for them to respond.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're upset, try the shape 'I felt ... when ...' instead of 'You made me ...'

quiz.question: Which sentence owns the feeling rather than blaming?
options: 'You made me furious.'
'Everyone is always against me.'
'You're so selfish.'
'I felt left out when I wasn't invited to lunch.'
quiz.explanation: Describing your own feeling and the event that triggered it is honest without accusing the other person.

cards.title: Kindness lives in how you say it, not in avoiding saying it
cards.body:
Some people think being direct means being blunt or cold. Others think being kind means staying quiet. But you can be clear and warm at the same time.

Kindness shows in small choices: picking a private moment, using the person's name, acknowledging their effort, and keeping your voice relaxed. 'I know you've been really busy, Sam, and I appreciate the help. I do need the report by Friday.' The message is firm, but the delivery is caring.

With a partner, 'I love our evenings together. I'd like us to put phones away at dinner' lands better than 'You're always on your phone.' The request is the same. The tone decides whether it feels like care or criticism.
cards.apply_it: Before raising something tricky today, add one genuine sentence of warmth or appreciation at the start.

quiz.question: What does 'kind' mean in saying what you mean kindly?
options: Saying it clearly with a warm, respectful delivery
Avoiding the difficult topic
Softening it until it's barely noticeable
Agreeing with whatever they say
quiz.explanation: Kindness is about how you deliver the message: warm and respectful, while still being clear.

cards.title: Let your voice and body back up your words
cards.body:
You can say all the right words, but if you mumble them while looking at the floor, people may not take them seriously. And if you say them through gritted teeth with arms folded, they'll hear anger.

Aim for a steady, normal-volume voice, relaxed shoulders and comfortable eye contact. Sit or stand facing the person. If you're on a video call, look at the camera when you make your key point.

Practising helps. Say your sentence out loud in the car or in front of a mirror: 'I'd like to leave at nine tomorrow.' Notice if your voice rises at the end as if it's a question. A level tone tells people you mean it.
cards.apply_it: Practise your next important sentence out loud once, checking your voice stays level and doesn't rise like a question at the end.

quiz.question: Why does body language matter when speaking assertively?
options: It doesn't; only the words count
It replaces the need to speak
If it doesn't match your words, people may doubt or misread you
It should always be very dramatic
quiz.explanation: People read tone and posture as well as words. When they match, your message is clearer and more believable.

cards.title: Expect some pushback and don't let guilt change your answer
cards.body:
When you start saying what you mean, not everyone will cheer. People used to your yes may sulk, argue or try guilt: 'I thought you were a team player', 'After all I've done for you.'

This is normal and doesn't mean you've done anything wrong. You can acknowledge their feeling without giving in: 'I can see you're disappointed. My answer is still no.' Stay calm and avoid getting dragged into a debate about whether you're a good person.

Give it time. Many people adjust once they realise your new clarity is here to stay. If someone consistently reacts badly to reasonable requests and boundaries, that tells you something useful about the relationship.
cards.apply_it: Prepare one calm reply for a guilt trip you often hear, such as 'I can see you're disappointed, and my answer is still no.'

quiz.question: Someone says, 'I thought you cared about me' after you decline a favour. What's an assertive reply?
options: 'Fine, I'll do it then.'
'How dare you say that!'
Say nothing and avoid them for a week
'I do care, and I still can't help this time.'
quiz.explanation: Acknowledging the relationship while keeping your answer shows care and clarity without giving in to guilt.

cards.title: Speaking up at work is part of doing the job well
cards.body:
In meetings and with managers, many people stay quiet because they don't want to seem difficult or ambitious. But silence can mean problems go unspotted, and your ideas and limits go unheard.

Try short, clear statements. 'I have a concern about the timeline.' 'I'd like to take the lead on the client pitch.' 'If I take this on, which current task should I pause?' That last one is a useful way to say no to more work without just refusing.

If speaking in a group is hard, prepare one point beforehand and aim to say it early, before nerves build. Or follow up in writing afterwards. Your voice adds value, and good teams need it.
cards.apply_it: Before your next meeting, prepare one point you'll make and aim to say it in the first ten minutes.

quiz.question: Your manager hands you another big task when you're already full. What's an assertive response?
options: Say yes and work late every night
'Happy to help. Which of my current tasks should I pause?'
Complain to colleagues later
Ignore the email
quiz.explanation: Asking which task to drop shows willingness while making your real capacity clear, so you both can prioritise.

cards.title: Start small, because assertiveness gets easier with practice
cards.body:
If you've been passive or people-pleasing for years, jumping straight to a big confrontation can feel terrifying. You don't have to.

Build up with low-stakes moments. Tell a waiter your meal is cold. Say which film you'd prefer instead of 'I don't mind'. Ask a shop assistant for help finding something. Each small act shows your brain that speaking up is survivable.

Expect it to feel awkward at first, even when you do it well. That discomfort is a sign you're doing something new, not something wrong. Over weeks, these small steps build the confidence for bigger conversations, like asking for a pay rise or telling a family member how you really feel.
cards.apply_it: Pick one low-stakes chance today to state a preference clearly, like choosing the restaurant or saying which film you'd like to watch.

quiz.question: What's a sensible way to build assertiveness if it feels hard?
options: Practise in small, low-stakes situations first
Start with the biggest conflict in your life
Wait until you feel no discomfort at all
Only practise in writing, never out loud
quiz.explanation: Small, low-risk practice builds confidence step by step, making bigger conversations easier later.

cards.title: A daily habit: say one clear, kind thing you'd normally avoid
cards.body:
Saying what you mean kindly comes down to a few habits: ask directly instead of hinting, say no without a long excuse, state boundaries as what you'll do, cut needless hedges and apologies, disagree with ideas rather than people, and name your feelings honestly.

To make it stick, try one small daily practice. Each evening, ask yourself: what did I want to say today but didn't? Then pick one similar moment tomorrow, and say it clearly and warmly in one or two sentences.

It might be asking a partner for help with dinner, telling a friend you'd prefer a different plan, or flagging a problem at work. Small, honest words, said kindly, add up to stronger relationships and less resentment.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write down one thing you held back today. Tomorrow, find a similar moment and say it clearly and kindly in one or two sentences.

quiz.question: Which daily practice best builds this skill?
options: Avoiding any conversation that feels awkward
Dropping more hints so people notice
Saying one clear, kind thing you'd usually hold back
Apologising before every request
quiz.explanation: Regularly saying one honest, kind thing you'd normally avoid builds the habit of clear, respectful communication.
